title: Catalog evidence storyboard and battle notes
body:
Executive summary:

This note proposes a storytelling-first approach (a short "storyboard") for how we present "verified profiles" in the Model Catalog, and provides sales-facing battle notes that translate our verification signals into defensible competitive claims. The goal is to make it easy for engineers and product leads to: 1) decide which open model to try, 2) understand where Redwood’s serving and evidence stack matters, and 3) get comfortable that a model marked as "verified" will behave predictably in production.

Primary audiences:
- Engineering leads evaluating model choices for chat/generation or retrieval-augmented workflows.
- Platform and infrastructure buyers (SRE/Platform teams) comparing inference economics and SLAs.
- Product managers and solution architects deciding on fidelity/cost tradeoffs.

Messaging objectives (what this doc must enable):
- Surface a compact claim hierarchy: headline benefit, 3 supporting predicates, and concrete evidence artifacts.
- Show where Redwood verification reduces buyer risk (quality regressions, latency surprises, hidden costs).
- Give sales a short set of battle-tested rebuttals against three competitor angles: pure API convenience, raw self-host performance vendors, and LLM marketplaces that emphasize model breadth over verification.
- Provide testable A/B copy and a simple evidence checklist for the catalog UI.

High-level claim hierarchy (storyboard frames):
1) Headline: "Pick confidently — models with verified performance & usage guidance."
2) Supporting predicate A (Quality): "Redwood verification ties model outputs to curated eval sets and regression guards so you won’t ship silent quality drops."
3) Supporting predicate B (Economics/Performance): "Verified profiles include expected latency & unit cost curves at common batch/seq lengths on our runtime."
4) Supporting predicate C (Fit): "Each profile includes recommended workloads, prompt patterns, and failure modes for production use."
5) Evidence artifacts (what we show on the profile page):
   - Small curated eval results (task-specific metrics with brief methodology notes)
   - A short "performance vignette" graph: 1, 8, 32 token latency and cost-per-token on Redwood Dedicated tier and Hosted baseline
   - Example prompt+response pairs for three use cases (good, borderline, failure)
   - Provenance + training-data heuristics (high-level, privacy-safe statement)
   - Known limitations and signal-to-noise guidance (where hallucinations spike, temperature sensitivity)

Narrative notes for the catalog UI and copy tests:
- Headline variants to A/B test on the profile page:
  A1: "Verified for production: quality signals, performance & usage tips."
  A2: "Open models you can trust—benchmarked and annotated for production."
  A3: "Pick the right open model fast: verified outputs, costs, and caveats."
- Quick explanatory blurbs (30–40 words) to appear under headline:
  "Every verified profile bundles lightweight evals, execution profiles, and recommended prompt patterns so your team can estimate cost and quality before committing."
- Microcopy for evidence badges (tooltip copy):
  "Eval-tested: contains a short task suite run by Redwood and the test harness used."
  "Perf-profile: real throughput & latency measured on Redwood runtimes at representative batch sizes."

Competitive claim map (three competitor angles and rebuttals):
1) "All-in convenience APIs" (competitor claim = "we have the most models and fast onboarding")
   - Redwood rebuttal: "We also have rapid onboarding, but our verified profiles reduce iteration time by surfacing the failure modes and expected unit economics up-front — reducing wasted spend and rollbacks."
   - Evidence to show: time-to-meaningful-eval metric (e.g., "minutes to run the curated 3-case suite"), customer quote that saved engineering hours, and perf previews.
2) "Self-host/Runtime sellers" (competitor claim = "you get maximum throughput & control if you host")
   - Redwood rebuttal: "Self-host can match performance but costs operational time. Our verified profiles pair runtime-optimized configs with model-fit guidance so customers get near-host performance with significantly less ops overhead."
   - Evidence to show: example config recipes, expected ops tasks avoided (list), and latency/cost deltas for the same model on Redwood Dedicated vs a baseline self-hosted config.
3) "Marketplaces/Model Hubs" (competitor claim = "breadth of models and community ratings")
   - Redwood rebuttal: "Breadth is useful; verification is how you reduce risk. Our catalog surfaces curated signals instead of noisy popularity metrics, and includes short failure examples so teams know what to test first."
   - Evidence to show: comparison snapshot highlighting verification fields vs star ratings, and a small case study of a team that avoided a high-impact regression by following Redwood guidance.

Sales battle notes (short snippets for reps):
- Quick opener for evaluation conversations: "We maintain lightweight verified profiles for open models—think of them as an engineering intake report: expected latency & token cost, quick evals on common tasks, and prompt patterns that work. Helps you scope a pilot in days, not weeks."
- Rebuttal for "speed over rigor" questions: "We can spin up a model path in minutes; the verified profile just adds 2–3 short checks that prevent expensive rollouts later."
- Objection handling for "we self-host and have infra": "Great — use our verified profile as the test plan and execution recipe. Many teams run the same checks locally but we save time by standardizing the test harness and providing tuned runtime knobs."

Evidence matrix (what we include on each profile and why):
- Task eval summary (short, reproducible): quick signal for quality. Why: engineers want a quick pass/fail.
- Perf snapshot (latency & cost at 3 points): quick signal for economics. Why: cost surprises kill pilots.
- Prompt patterns and sample best/worst outputs: quick signal for fit. Why: shows boundary conditions and real examples.
- Verification date + rig run id (immutable reference): signal for freshness. Why: models change; buyers want to know when the check was done.
- Known limitations paragraph: builds trust through honesty.

UX considerations (catalog page layout suggestions):
- Top strip: headline + 3 evidence badges (Eval-tested, Perf-profile, Recommended workloads) with tooltips.
- Middle: two-column layout — left column: short narrative + top 3 quick metrics; right column: sample prompt/responses carousel.
- Bottom: expandable details — full eval methodology, runtime config snippets, and a changelog for the profile.

A/B test ideas and success metrics:
- A/B test 1: Headline variant A1 vs A2 on catalog page. Metric: clicks to "Start trial" and "Add to sandbox".
- A/B test 2: Badge visibility (show badges vs hide). Metric: reduction in pilot time (self-reported in follow-up survey) and increased "download eval kit" events.
- A/B test 3: Include a one-sentence failure example vs none. Metric: lead quality (MQL->SQL conversion) and reduction in early-stage support tickets for "unexpected outputs".

Short verification checklist (for the profile owner role):
- Run curated task suite (3–5 tasks) and capture scores + seed configs.
- Measure latency/cost at seq lengths [1, 16, 256] with batch sizes [1, 8, 32].
- Capture 3 exemplar prompt/response pairs (best, borderline, failure).
- Write a 2–3 sentence known-limits section and list recommended temperature/top-p ranges.
- Note data provenance high-level statement and date of verification run.

Risks & open questions:
- How deep should the provenance guidance be without overstepping privacy/regulatory boundaries? (Requires alignment with legal.)
- Who owns profile freshness? We need a cadence and an auto-expiry UI signal for profiles older than X months.
- How do we surface negative evidence without deterring experimentation? Tone and microcopy matter here.

Next steps (owner: Priya + product):
1) Run the verification checklist for 5 high-interest open models and publish as "pilot verified" profiles (due: 2025-02-01).
2) Build a small profile UI mock (headlines, badges, sample panel) and run internal heuristics testing with SEs (due: 2025-01-22).
3) Draft 3 sales battlecards from this doc and circulate to Revenue for feedback (due: 2025-01-30).

Appendix: sample short sales snippets for rep playbook (one-liners):
- "If you want predictable costs and fewer surprises, start with a verified profile — it tells you how the model behaves on our runtime and where to test first."
- "Verified profiles are intentionally lightweight: they save engineering time by surfacing the 2–3 failure modes we see most often for a given workload."

End of note.
